accuracy.evidence: Checked against NGSS 1-ESS1-1 and its clarification statement (sun and moon appear to rise in one part of the sky, move across and set; stars other than the sun are visible at night but not in the day), NASA Science 'Moon Phases' (synodic month about 29.5 days; new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full and the waning sequence) and the National Curriculum in England Year 1 seasonal change. The lab draws the waxing Moon lit on the right as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, and the adult text says so; it notes the Sun rises roughly east and sets roughly west, exactly so only near the equinoxes, and that the Sun only seems to move because Earth turns. The day-sky Moon is drawn as a half moon, which matches the first-quarter Moon being up in the afternoon.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-years sky misconceptions (Vosniadou and Brewer; Trundle, Atwood and Christopher on lunar phases): stars go away or switch off in the day (prediction 2, challenge 'gone', p3, m4), the Moon is only out at night (prediction 4, sort item 'the Moon' in Both, 'night', m2), the Moon changes from new to full overnight or takes a year ('jump', 'day', 'year'), the Sun sets where it rose (prediction 1, 'same', p1, m5) and stars come out at the same time all year ('summer', m8). The adult text warns against the clouds-or-shadow explanation of phases.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagmoonph is built on sky patterns over time: a Sun dragged along a dashed east-to-west arc with the sky colour following its height, a day-to-night slider where stars fade in and a Turn off the sky glow button shows them in daylight, a 30-night strip that fills in with drawn Moon phases computed from the cycle, an ordering board for five phase cards, and a Day/Night/Both sort. flagsky sorts day and night pictures and turns a seasons wheel; flagstar is about the Sun being a star. Neither draws phases or a month. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees each pattern happen before the text names it: the sky turns orange and the label reads sunset only on the west side; stars appear as the sky darkens and the glow-off view shows they were there at midday; stepping nights makes the lit part grow to full and then shrink, filling the month strip; a wrong card in the order board is outlined in red with 'look for the shape with a little less light'.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab disproves: 'the same side' for sunset (the Sun ends in the west), 'they go away' for daytime stars (the glow-off view shows them), 'gets smaller' or 'stays the same' after new moon (the strip grows), and 'No, never' for a daytime Moon (the pale half moon is in the day sky in step 2 and sorts into Both).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with eight distinct feedback messages naming the slip: setting in the east, the Sun staying up, stars going away, the Moon jumping back to full, a one-day cycle, a one-year cycle, the Moon only at night, and stars at the same time all year. Answer order rotates.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses very short sentences and everyday words (comes up, goes down, thin slice, grows, shrinks) with sunrise, sunset, east and west each explained once; adult text names NGSS 1-ESS1-1 and the phase vocabulary. Canvas labels are one or two words (sunrise, Night, Day 7: half moon). validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph covers one pattern (the Sun's daily path, stars hidden by day, the monthly Moon, the Moon in the day sky). Items mix reasoning types: counting on to the next full moon (p2, p4, m3), reading the time of day from the Sun's position (m5), ordering phases (m1, m6), counting nights in weeks of a Moon diary (m7) and the seasonal link to star time (m8).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step after Show me. Night-sky scenes use fixed dark colours with white chips so they read the same in both themes; buttons are full-size lbtn (44 px+), five phase cards fit across 360 px at about 60 px each, the East and West chips stay inside the canvas, and the 30-night strip has Next night and One week on buttons as large-target alternatives to dragging.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a labelled button twin: Later and Earlier for the Sun and for day to night, Turn off the sky glow, Next night, One week on and Back to day 0, one button per Moon shape, and Day, Night and Both. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (time of day and where the Sun is, whether stars show, day number and Moon shape, which card fits next). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: NGSS 1-ESS1-1 Earth's Place in the Universe, performance expectation and clarification statement (NGSS Lead States, 2013)
NASA Science, Moon Phases (moon.nasa.gov), synodic month and phase names
National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 1 seasonal changes (DfE 2013)
Trundle, K. C., Atwood, R. K. and Christopher, J. E., Preservice elementary teachers' conceptions of moon phases (Journal of Research in Science Teaching, 2002), common phase misconceptions
